CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chest pain, resolved; referred from emergency department for evaluation of possible esophagitis.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a new patient referred from the emergency department. She reports experiencing chest pain in early October 2020 lasting four days. Pain was sharp, located in the center of her chest behind the breastbone, and she felt it was consistent with a heart attack. The pain occurred randomly without waking her and was worse with eating. She tolerated it for four days before going to the emergency room when nothing relieved it. In the ER, she underwent EKG and blood tests, all of which were normal, and was not prescribed any medications. She also experienced associated difficulty swallowing. Both the chest pain and swallowing difficulty resolved approximately three days after the ER visit. She has been completely asymptomatic for the past three months since this initial episode. Patient notes she was undergoing a stressful job transition at the time her symptoms occurred. She denies abdominal pain and reports normal bowel movements. She is currently attempting to lose weight.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies prior history of heartburn. Pain exacerbated by eating. Associated dysphagia, now resolved. No abdominal pain. Normal bowel movements. Denies family history of gastrointestinal problems.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Uterine fibroids
Anemia
Cholecystectomy (several years ago)

MEDICATIONS
Not documented

ALLERGIES
Not documented

FAMILY HISTORY
Denies family history of gastrointestinal problems.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Recent stressful job transition coinciding with onset of symptoms. Currently attempting weight loss.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: Soft, non-distended. Mild tenderness to light palpation in bilateral upper abdominal quadrants, approximately equal distribution. No tenderness to palpation in lower abdomen. No other significant abnormalities.

RESULTS
Emergency department workup: EKG normal. Cardiac workup normal. Blood tests normal.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Three-month history of resolved acute chest pain with associated dysphagia from October 2020. Differential diagnosis includes GERD, dyspepsia, esophagitis, musculoskeletal etiologies, and anxiety. Most likely etiology is anxiety related to job stress with possible musculoskeletal contribution. If esophagitis was present, likely already healed given prolonged asymptomatic period.

Plan: Discussed EGD (upper endoscopy) versus conservative management with symptom monitoring. Given the three-month asymptomatic period, explained that any esophagitis would likely have healed and EGD would likely not reveal findings. Patient elected to defer EGD and self-monitor symptoms. Instructed to call office if she experiences recurrent chest pain or other concerning symptoms, at which time EGD can be performed. Will follow up as needed for any additional gastrointestinal complaints.
